lesson.title: Current in a single loop
lesson.orientation: Trace the wire from one battery terminal through the resistor until it reaches the other terminal.

visualBrief.learningPurpose: Show one closed circuit and the direction used to describe conventional current.
facts: The wire forms one closed path.
The battery supplies a potential difference.
The resistor is in series with the battery.
Current has the same value at every point in this ideal single loop.

objects.name: Resistor
objects.description: One resistor placed in the loop.

visualBrief.altTextDraft: A battery and resistor are connected by one closed wire loop. An arrow on the top wire shows conventional current around the loop.
verificationChecks: The voltage, resistance, and calculated current agree with Ohm's law.

lesson.reviewLabel: Voltage against current in one loop
lesson.nextAction: Open the next lesson to see what happens when a second resistor joins the same path.

stageTitles.review: Recall what a single loop does

steps.headline: Current is how much charge passes a point each second.

lead.text: Think of litres per second through a pipe. Electric current is the same idea for charge. It is a rate, not an amount waiting somewhere to be used.
One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point every second.
Now the real circuit: one battery, one resistor and one loop of wire.
A meter on the wire counts the charge passing it each second. One meter goes just before the resistor, another just after.

reveal.text: The same. You saw it with the water: a closed loop gives charge one route, and nothing leaves or piles up.
In a single loop the current is the same everywhere, including on both sides of the resistor.

steps.headline: Ohm's law sets the current: voltage divided by resistance.

lead.text: The push is the voltage V, in volts. The opposition is the resistance R, in ohms (Ω). Ohm's law joins them:
Make R bigger and the same battery drives less current. For example, 9 V across 90 Ω gives 0.1 A.

steps.headline: A 9 V battery is connected across a 450 Ω resistor. Find the current.

workedSteps.text: Write Ohm's law for the current.
Substitute the battery voltage and the resistance.

steps.headline: A 6 V battery is connected across a 150 Ω resistor. Find the current.

workedSteps.text: Write Ohm's law for the current.
Substitute the battery voltage and the resistance.

lead.text: Same shape as the last two. This time you do all of it.

reveal.text: Voltage over resistance, every time. Volts divided by ohms gives amperes.

lead.text: The same loop, with new numbers. The current is still set by the whole loop, and a meter reads it anywhere along the wire.

visualStates.caption: One battery and one resistor on a single loop. No values yet.

blocks.text: Water is pumped round a closed loop of pipe. Halfway round, the pipe narrows. Every second, 2 litres pass a mark before the narrow section. The pipe doesn't leak.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the current in a single loop from its voltage and resistance, and say why it is the same everywhere.

recap.keyIdea: Current is the rate charge passes a point. In a single loop it is the same everywhere, and Ohm's law sets it: current equals voltage divided by resistance.

blocks.text: You found that 5 V across 100 Ω drives 0.05 A, and that a meter after a resistor reads what a meter before it reads.

recap.nextHook: Add a second resistor to the loop. Does the current change, and by how much?

questions.prompt: A single-loop circuit has a fixed resistor. Which change increases the current?
hints: Write down I = V / R and look at which quantity each option changes.
Raising the denominator lowers the result; raising the numerator raises it.
Decide which option raises the numerator of I = V / R.

choices.label: Adding a second resistor along the same path
Replacing the resistor with a larger one

questions.onCorrect: More voltage on the top of V ÷ R raises the current. More resistance of any kind lowers it.

misconceptions.feedback: A second resistor on the same path adds opposition. That lowers the current.
A larger resistor sits underneath in V ÷ R. That lowers the current.
Longer wire adds a little opposition. It cannot raise the current.

questions.prompt: A 5 V battery is connected across a 100 Ω resistor. What is the current, in amperes?
hints: Which two values does Ohm's law divide?
Voltage goes on top and resistance underneath.
Work out 5 ÷ 100 and read the answer in amperes.

transfer.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected across a 200 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in amperes.

questions.onCorrect: 0.05 A. Voltage divided by resistance, and volts over ohms gives amperes.

misconceptions.feedback: You divided the resistance by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.
That multiplies the two values. More resistance should lower the current, not raise it.

questions.prompt: Calculate I = 6 V ÷ 150 Ω, in amperes.
hints: Divide the voltage by the resistance.
The voltage is smaller than the resistance, so the answer is less than 1.
Work out 6 ÷ 150. Try 600 ÷ 150 first, then move the decimal point.
questions.onCorrect: 0.04 A. Six volts across 150 Ω pushes a small current, because the resistance is large.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the resistance divided by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.
That multiplies the two values. A resistor holds the current back, so multiplying can't be right.

questions.prompt: A single-loop circuit contains one battery and one resistor. Explain why the current is the same on both sides of the resistor.
hints: Think about how many routes the charge has around this circuit.
Ask what would have to happen to the charge for the two values to differ.
Say what the single path implies about the rate of flow at any two points.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: There is only one path, so the same current passes every point in it. Charge is not used up by the resistor; the resistor limits the rate of flow rather than consuming the charge.

questions.onCorrect: One path, so charge passing one point must pass the next. The resistor limits the rate; it does not use up charge.

questions.prompt: How many litres pass a mark after the narrow section each second?
hints: Where could the water go if the pipe doesn't leak?
If more arrived than left, what would pile up?
Whatever passes the first mark each second must also pass the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing leaks and nothing builds up, so 2 litres pass the second mark each second.

questions.onCorrect: 2 litres. Nothing leaks or piles up in a closed loop, so the flow is the same at every mark.

misconceptions.feedback: Water would have to vanish in the narrow part. Where would the missing water go?
The pump keeps pushing, so some water always passes. Think about what the narrow section can and can't do.

questions.prompt: A meter just before the resistor reads 0.05 A. What does an identical meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: How did this compare with the water in the pipe?
Could any charge leave the wire inside the resistor?
Count the routes charge has around the loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One path, so the current is the same on both sides: 0.05 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.05 A. One path means one current: every point on the loop passes the same charge each second.

misconceptions.feedback: A resistor holds the flow back but the loop is still carrying current. What would happen to charge that stopped arriving?
Half would mean charge vanished in the resistor. A resistor limits the flow of the whole loop; it does not consume charge.

questions.prompt: Why does Ohm's law divide the voltage by the resistance?
hints: Think about what a bigger resistance does to the flow.
If R grows, should the current grow or shrink?

acceptedIdeas: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current.

choices.label: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
A bigger resistance pushes harder, so it gives a bigger current
Resistance and voltage are measured in the same unit

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by R makes a bigger resistance give a smaller current. That is what opposition means.

misconceptions.feedback: Resistance opposes the flow; it does not push. Ask which way the current should move when R grows.
Volts and ohms are different units. The question is about what resistance does to the flow.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a loop with one 60 Ω resistor. What does a meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: What does Ohm's law give for the whole loop?
In a single loop the current is the same at every point.
Work out 12 ÷ 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 60 Ω = 0.2 A, and the current is the same on both sides of the resistor.

questions.onCorrect: 0.2 A. Ohm's law gives the loop's current, and the same current passes every point in it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the voltage by the resistance. A resistor lowers the current, so the answer should be small.
You divided the resistance by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.

questions.prompt: A 10 V supply drives a single loop containing one 400 Ω resistor. Calculate the current, in amperes.
hints: Which value goes on top in Ohm's law?
Divide the supply voltage by the resistance.
Work out 10 ÷ 400. It is less than 0.1.
questions.onCorrect: 0.025 A. Voltage over resistance, and 400 Ω is a lot of opposition for 10 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.
That multiplies the two values. More resistance means less current.

hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: How much charge passes a point each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much charge passes a point each second

choices.label: How much charge passes a point each second
How much charge is stored in the wire

questions.onCorrect: Current is a rate: charge passing a point each second, in amperes.

misconceptions.feedback: Current is not stored in the wire. It is charge moving past a point.
How hard the battery pushes is the voltage. Current is the flow that results.

hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?
questions.onCorrect: Voltage divided by resistance: a bigger resistance gives a smaller current.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying would make more resistance give more current. Resistance holds the current back.
That puts the resistance on top. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.
